title: Berkshire 2017 letter: the Protégé bet, float, leverage aversion, and acquisition discipline
summary: Buffett reviews 2017, warning about distorting GAAP rules and frenzied acquisition pricing, explaining insurance float and mega-cat preparedness, and settling his ten-year S&P 500 index fund bet against hedge funds. Core lessons: avoid leverage, ignore short-term price noise, favor big easy decisions, and bonds can be riskier than stocks over long horizons.

principles.text: Never risk what you have and need to obtain what you don't need; avoiding leverage lets you sleep well.
principles.quote: Both of us believe it is insane to risk what you have and need in order to obtain what you don’t need.

principles.text: Evaluate acquisitions on an all-equity basis and ignore forecast synergies; cheap debt and CEO enthusiasm inflate deal prices.
principles.quote: At Berkshire, in contrast, we evaluate acquisitions on an all-equity basis

principles.text: Seek durable competitive strengths, able management, good returns on tangible assets, growth, and a sensible price.
principles.quote: the key qualities we seek are durable competitive strengths; able and high-grade management; good returns on the net tangible assets required to operate the business

principles.text: Insurance float is money held for others that Berkshire invests; underwriting discipline can make its cost negative, but it carries oceans of risk.
principles.quote: The downside of float is that it comes with risk, sometimes oceans of risk.

principles.text: Never depend on the kindness of strangers; hold ample liquidity like Treasury Bills to withstand crises.
principles.quote: Charlie and I never will operate Berkshire in a manner that depends on the kindness of strangers

principles.text: Treat stocks as business interests; short-term prices are a voting machine, long-term a weighing machine.
principles.quote: “In the short run, the market is a voting machine; in the long run, however, it becomes a weighing machine.”
